chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: There is no such thing as a digital arrest
chunks.text:
No law lets anyone arrest you over a call.
Nobody in India can arrest you through a phone call or a video call. There is no such procedure. The words "digital arrest" were invented by criminals. If a caller says you are under arrest and must stay on the call, that caller is a thief, not an officer.
Police, CBI, ED, customs and the courts do not work this way. They do not question people over video call. They do not keep someone online for hours. They do not tell you to hide the call from your family. And no real officer will ever ask you to send money to prove that you are innocent.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: There is no such thing as a digital arrest
chunks.text:
The stories these callers use.
The story changes, the plan stays the same. You may hear that a parcel in your name was caught with drugs, that your bank account or SIM was used for money laundering, or that a case has been filed against you in a far-off city. Some callers wear a uniform on camera. Some show a room made to look like a police station or a court.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: There is no such thing as a digital arrest
chunks.text:
Then comes the real ask. They tell you to move your savings to a "verification account" or an "RBI account" and promise to send it back after the checking is over. That money is gone the moment you send it. RBI does not keep anyone's money in such an account.
What to do while the call is happening.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: There is no such thing as a digital arrest
chunks.text:
- Cut the call. You are allowed to hang up. Nothing bad happens because you did.
- Do not switch on your camera, and do not move the call to another app.
- Do not send money to any account, no matter how official the reason sounds.
- Tell one family member or neighbour right away. Secrecy is this scam's main tool.
- Call 1930, the national cybercrime helpline, and file a report on cybercrime.gov.in.
If you have already paid.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: There is no such thing as a digital arrest
chunks.text:
Call 1930 the same day, even at night. The sooner the bank and the police know, the better the chance of stopping the money. Report it on cybercrime.gov.in as well, and keep the call records, the account number you paid to, and any screenshots.
Being frightened by such a call is normal. These callers are trained to frighten people. Nobody thinks clearly while a stranger is shouting about jail. If you are unsure, take your phone to your bank branch or the nearest police station and show them everything before you do anything else.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: Fake KYC alerts, prize offers and remote access apps
chunks.text:
The KYC message that wants you to hurry.
A message arrives saying your KYC has expired and your account will be blocked today. It gives a link to tap, or tells you to install an app to finish the KYC. Banks do not close accounts by SMS, and they do not send a link to fix your KYC.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: Fake KYC alerts, prize offers and remote access apps
chunks.text:
Look at the link before you believe it. Real bank addresses are short and end with the bank's own name. Scam links are shortened so you cannot see where they go, or they wrap the bank's name inside a longer address, or they change one letter so the page only looks like the bank's page. If your KYC is really due, your branch will tell you at the counter or on a call you can check for yourself.
The prize that asks you for money.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: Fake KYC alerts, prize offers and remote access apps
chunks.text:
You are told you have won a lottery, a lucky draw, a phone, or a job in another city. First you must send a small processing fee, a courier charge, a customs duty, or a registration amount. There is no prize and there is no job. The fee is the scam. After the first payment the caller will ask for a second one, then a third.
A genuine prize never needs money from the winner. A genuine employer never asks you to pay to be hired.
Apps, screen sharing and APK files.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: Fake KYC alerts, prize offers and remote access apps
chunks.text:
A caller says he is a bank executive and wants to help you. He asks you to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer, QuickSupport or a similar app so he can see your screen. Once it is on, he can watch you type your PIN and can operate your phone himself. Other scammers send a file on WhatsApp whose name ends in .apk and ask you to install it. Such a file can read your SMS and take your OTPs.
What to do.

chunks.source: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
chunks.title: Fake KYC alerts, prize offers and remote access apps
chunks.text:
- Do not open a link that came with a KYC warning. Open your own bank app, or walk into the branch.
- Never install an app because a caller told you to, and never install a file sent on WhatsApp.
- Never pay a fee to receive a prize, a refund, or a job.
- If you already installed a screen sharing app, uninstall it, turn off your phone's internet, and call your bank.
- Report the number and the message on 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in, and keep the message as proof.

chunks.title: You never enter your UPI PIN to receive money
chunks.text:
The one rule that never changes.
Your UPI PIN only sends money out. It never brings money in.
Money coming into your account needs nothing from you. No PIN, no OTP, no approval, no new app. It simply arrives and your bank sends you a credit message. So if anyone says "enter your PIN to receive the refund" or "approve this and your prize money will come", that person is taking money out of your account, not putting it in. This is true on PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, BHIM and every other UPI app.
What this trap looks like on your phone.

chunks.title: You never enter your UPI PIN to receive money
chunks.text: The scammer uses a collect request. It is a normal UPI feature that lets one person ask another for money. Used as a trap, it looks like this:

chunks.title: You never enter your UPI PIN to receive money
chunks.text:
1. A notification arrives, such as "Payment request received" or "Rahul is requesting Rs. 25,000".
2. You open the app and see a large PAY or ACCEPT button.
3. The sender's name may read "SBI Refund", "Cashback", "OLX Delivery" or "Insurance Claim". Anyone can type that name into their own profile. Your bank does not check it.
4. If you press pay, the app asks for your four or six digit UPI PIN.
5. The moment you enter the PIN, the money leaves your account. It cannot be pulled back.
Check these things before you press anything.

chunks.title: You never enter your UPI PIN to receive money
chunks.text:
- Read the direction word on the screen. "Paying", "Pay", "Debit" or "Sending" all mean money is leaving your account.
- Treat every PIN screen as a payment screen. There is no exception.
- Look at the amount. It is usually the exact sum you were promised as a refund or prize.
- Do not trust the display name. Tell the person to just send the money, then wait for your bank's credit SMS.
- If you did not ask anyone for money, decline the request and block that UPI ID.
If you have already entered your PIN.

chunks.title: You never enter your UPI PIN to receive money
chunks.text:
- Open the transaction in your UPI app and use Report or Raise Dispute, then block the sender's UPI ID.
- Call your bank on the number printed on the back of your ATM card or in your passbook and ask them to raise a UPI dispute.
- Call 1930, the national cybercrime helpline, the same day. Money reported in the first few hours is easiest to freeze.
- File a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in with the UPI ID, the amount and the transaction reference number.
- Never pay again to "release" or "unblock" the first payment. That is the same scam continuing.

chunks.title: Loan apps, recovery threats and how to borrow safely
chunks.text:
Money runs short in every household. Needing a loan is normal and it is nothing to be ashamed of. This page is only about telling a real lender apart from a trap.
Borrow only from a lender the RBI regulates.
In India a loan can legally be given only by a bank or by a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) registered with the Reserve Bank of India. An app is not a lender. An app is only a shopfront for one.

chunks.title: Loan apps, recovery threats and how to borrow safely
chunks.text:
Before you accept any money, the app must tell you in writing which bank or NBFC is actually giving the loan, the full rate of interest, and every fee. If the app will not name its lender, walk away. Ask for the loan agreement before the money reaches you, not after. A genuine lender gives it without argument. You can check whether a company is registered on the RBI website, rbi.org.in.
Apps that ask for your contacts and your photos.

chunks.title: Loan apps, recovery threats and how to borrow safely
chunks.text:
A real loan app does not need your phone contacts, your photo gallery, or your camera to decide your loan. An app that demands these permissions is collecting people it can threaten later.
Never install a screen-sharing or remote-control app such as AnyDesk, TeamViewer or QuickSupport because a loan officer asked you to. That hands a stranger full control of your phone and your bank app.
Threats and morphed photos are a crime.

chunks.title: Loan apps, recovery threats and how to borrow safely
chunks.text:
Some recovery agents abuse borrowers, call their relatives, or paste a borrower's face onto an obscene picture and send it to their contacts. Be clear about this: that is a criminal offence committed against you. It is not part of any loan. Even if you genuinely owe money, no one is permitted to do it. You have not done anything wrong, and the shame belongs entirely to the person sending those messages.
What to do.

chunks.title: Loan apps, recovery threats and how to borrow safely
chunks.text:
- Stop paying anything that is demanded by threat. Pay only into the lender's official account, exactly as written in your agreement.
- Do not delete the calls, messages or images. Take screenshots. They are your evidence.
- Report it on the cybercrime helpline 1930, or online at cybercrime.gov.in.
- File a written complaint at your local police station and keep a stamped copy.
- Complain against the lender on the RBI Sachet portal, sachet.rbi.org.in.
- Tell one family member or neighbour today. Facing it alone is exactly what the agent is counting on.

chunks.title: Never share OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone
chunks.text:
Some numbers belong only to you.
Your OTP belongs only to you. So does your ATM PIN, your UPI PIN, the three-digit
CVV on the back of your card, your full card number and your internet banking
password.
A real bank employee never needs any of these from you. The bank already has your
account details on its own computer. So if someone on a call or on WhatsApp asks
you for these numbers, that person does not work for your bank, whatever name or
post they give.
This stays true even when the caller sounds convincing:

chunks.title: Never share OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone
chunks.text:
- The caller already knows your name, your village or part of your account number.
- The message came from a number or a sender name that looks official.
- The caller says your account will be blocked in ten minutes.
- The caller says they are calling from the Reserve Bank of India.
The Reserve Bank of India does not call customers.
RBI is the bank for banks. It does not open accounts for ordinary people. It has
no reason to phone you, message you, or send you a link about your account, KYC
or money. Anyone who says "I am from RBI" and then asks for a number or a
transfer is lying to you.

chunks.title: Never share OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone
chunks.text:
What to do when such a call or message comes.
- Do not say any secret number out loud, not even one digit.
- Cut the call. You do not owe politeness to a stranger who is pressuring you.
- Turn your ATM card over and call the customer care number printed on the back,
  or the number printed inside your passbook. Use only that number.
- If you are still unsure, walk into your branch and ask at the counter.
- Never open a link sent in a message about your account. Use only the bank app
  you already installed.
Hurry is itself the warning sign.

chunks.title: Never share OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone
chunks.text:
Real bank work is never a ten-minute emergency. Blocking a card, restarting KYC
and getting a refund can all wait until you have checked. Fear and hurry are the
caller's tools, so slowing down breaks the trick.
If you have already shared an OTP, a PIN or a card number, act the same day. Call
your bank on the number on your card and ask them to block the card or freeze the
account. Then report it on the national cybercrime helpline 1930, or at
cybercrime.gov.in. Reporting fast gives the bank the best chance of stopping the
money. You have done nothing wrong by being tricked.
